name: Weight Function Invariant and Worst-Case Distribution Lower Bound
description: When moving pieces on a 3D grid toward the origin by repeatedly merging pieces along each coordinate axis using distinct merging bases and shifting one step in the negative direction, define a weight function for each point as the reciprocal of the product of powers of the merging bases: increasing the coordinate by 1 along an axis divides the weight by that axis's base. Each operation preserves the total weight sum. Since a single piece at the origin has weight 1, the initial total weight must be at least 1. The worst initial distribution piles all pieces at the farthest corner from the origin, yielding an exact lower bound on the minimum total number of pieces required to guarantee reachability; a greedy moving sequence can achieve this bound.
applicability: Process problems involving merging by different multiples and moving toward a fixed point
When merging bases are pairwise coprime integers, a weight function in the form of a product of powers naturally makes the operation conserved
The argument proceeds in two steps: necessity (weight sum invariant) and sufficiency (constructing reachability)

steps.step: Define the weight function on the 3D grid
steps.detail: Let the three coordinate axes have distinct merging bases a, b, c. For a grid point (x, y, z) with non-negative integer coordinates, define its weight as w(x, y, z) = 1/(a^x b^y c^z). Thus increasing a coordinate by 1 along an axis divides the weight by the corresponding base.

steps.step: Show the total weight sum is invariant under each operation
steps.detail: An operation merges pieces along one axis (say the x-axis) using base a and shifts them one step toward the negative direction. Because the weight function is defined as the reciprocal of the product of powers of the bases, the total weight sum before and after the operation remains unchanged. The same holds for operations along the y- and z-axes.

steps.step: Derive the necessary lower bound from the invariant
steps.detail: A single piece at the origin (0, 0, 0) has weight w(0, 0, 0) = 1. Since the total weight is invariant, any initial configuration that can eventually produce a piece at the origin must have total weight at least 1.

steps.step: Identify the worst-case initial distribution
steps.detail: The worst distribution—requiring the largest number of pieces to achieve total weight ≥ 1—is to place all pieces at the farthest corner of the grid from the origin. This gives the exact lower bound on the minimum total number of pieces needed to guarantee reachability.

steps.step: Prove sufficiency by constructing a greedy sequence
steps.detail: A greedy merging-and-moving sequence (always merge when possible along any axis toward the origin) can achieve the lower bound derived from the worst-case distribution, proving the bound is tight.

name: Fibonacci and Lucas Identity-Based Minimal Difference Cover
description: Strategy for finding the smallest integer set whose pairwise differences cover all Fibonacci number differences over a given index interval (plus an accompanying Lucas number difference). Core identity: the difference of two consecutive even-index Fibonacci numbers equals the middle odd-index term, F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1}. Therefore, including 0 and all even-index Fibonacci numbers in the set allows adjacent differences to cover all target odd-index terms; Lucas numbers can also be rewritten as differences of two Fibonacci numbers. Minimality is derived from the fact that endpoint differences can only be expressed via adjacent even-index terms—removing the outermost elements makes the endpoint differences unrepresentable. Common pitfalls: forgetting the adjacent even-index difference identity; including odd-index terms in the set, making it larger than necessary; proving minimality by counting alone rather than by non-representability.
applicability: Problems involving Fibonacci/Lucas numbers where index parity-related identities are relevant
Problems requiring a set of integers whose differences cover a specified target set of values
Problems asking for the minimum/smallest/least such covering set

steps.step: List relevant Fibonacci and Lucas identities tied to index parity
steps.detail: Write down identities such as F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1} and expressions of Lucas numbers as differences of Fibonacci numbers. These connect even-index elements to the odd-index differences they must cover.

steps.step: Construct the candidate covering set using 0 and even-index Fibonacci numbers
steps.detail: Include 0 and all even-index Fibonacci numbers within the relevant index range. By the identity F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1}, adjacent differences in this set produce every required odd-index Fibonacci difference. Any required Lucas difference can also be represented as a difference of two Fibonacci numbers, hence covered by the set.

steps.step: Prove minimality via endpoint non-representability
steps.detail: Show that the extreme (endpoint) differences can only be obtained from the outermost even-index elements. If the outermost element is removed, the corresponding endpoint difference becomes unrepresentable. Therefore no proper subset can still cover all required differences. Avoid relying solely on counting arguments.

name: Decimal Digit Operations and Divisibility Strategies
description: This module records two reusable strategies for decimal digit manipulation problems involving divisibility. (a) Distinct-digit 'deletion-divisible' numbers: starting from one-digit seeds, iteratively append digits to build larger numbers such that the new number is an integer multiple of the previous number and deleting one specific digit recovers the previous number. The deletion operation must not create leading zeros, and the resulting number must retain the distinct-digit property. The maximum such number is verified by an explicit deletion chain where each step removes some digit (the digit and position may vary per step) to obtain the number from the prior step. (b) Divisibility patterns of digit sums over consecutive integers: when no carry occurs, the digit sum modulo a given prime p increases by 1 at each step; when a carry occurs across a block of consecutive 9s, the digit sum drops sharply. Determining that 'every digit sum within a fixed-length segment is not divisible by p' is equivalent to avoiding intervals where the digit sum lands on a multiple of p. Minimality is verified via digit-sum dynamic programming or segment-by-segment scanning. General problem-solving route: for digit-operation problems, first clarify the legal rules for 'deleting a digit' (deleting the leading digit is forbidden if it creates a leading zero); the '+1 increment, sharp drop on carry' pattern of digit sums modulo p is the key tool for locating forbidden segments; 'product not divisible' should first be reduced to 'every factor is not divisible'.
applicability: Constructing or searching for distinct-digit numbers where deleting one digit yields a divisor of the original number, and the property can be iterated.
Verifying the maximum such number via an explicit deletion chain.
Analyzing whether digit sums of consecutive integers over a fixed interval are all not divisible by a given prime p.
Locating forbidden intervals where digit sum ≡ 0 (mod p) using the +1 increment and carry-drop pattern.
Reducing 'product not divisible by p' to checking each factor individually.

steps.step: Define legal digit deletion rules
steps.detail: When deleting a digit from a decimal number, the operation is illegal if it creates a leading zero (e.g., deleting the first digit of a number whose second digit is 0). The resulting number must also preserve the distinct-digit property if required by the problem.

steps.step: Construct deletion-divisible numbers by iterative expansion
steps.detail: Start from one-digit seed numbers. For each current number n with distinct digits, try appending a digit d (0–9, not already in n) to form a new number n' such that n' is an integer multiple of n (i.e., n' = k·n for some integer k ≥ 2) and there exists a digit in n' whose deletion yields back n. Continue expanding until no further valid extension is possible. Use branching search (e.g., Python recursion/backtracking) rather than seeking a closed-form analytic expression.

steps.step: Verify the maximum deletion-divisible number via an explicit deletion chain
steps.detail: To confirm a candidate maximum number, exhibit a deletion chain: a sequence of numbers starting from the candidate down to a one-digit number, where each step deletes exactly one digit (digit and position may differ per step) to obtain the previous number. At every step verify (i) the divisibility relation (the larger number is a multiple of the smaller), and (ii) all digits in each number are distinct.

steps.step: Model digit sum modulo p behavior over consecutive integers
steps.detail: Let p be a given prime. When incrementing an integer by 1, if no carry occurs (i.e., the last digit is not 9), the digit sum increases by 1, so digit sum modulo p increases by 1 modulo p. If a carry occurs across a block of t consecutive trailing 9s, the digit sum drops by 9t – 1 (since the 9s become 0s and the digit before them increases by 1). This creates a sharp drop in the digit sum modulo p.

steps.step: Identify forbidden intervals for digit sum divisibility
steps.detail: A segment of consecutive integers all have digit sums not divisible by p if and only if the segment avoids all positions where the digit sum lands on a multiple of p. Scan the integer line segment by segment, using the +1 increment and carry-drop pattern to mark intervals where digit sum ≡ 0 (mod p); the complement gives the allowed segments.

steps.step: Verify minimality via digit-sum DP or segment scanning
steps.detail: To prove a certain length is minimal (e.g., the shortest interval guaranteeing a digit sum divisible by p), either run a digit-sum dynamic programming over the relevant range or scan consecutive blocks explicitly, checking that every shorter interval can avoid the forbidden multiples while the claimed length cannot.

steps.step: Reduce product non-divisibility to factor-wise checks
steps.detail: If a problem asks that a product of several integers is not divisible by a prime p, this is equivalent to requiring that none of the individual factors is divisible by p. Do not confuse 'product not divisible' with the negation of 'each factor divisible'.

name: Linear Programming Duality: Construction Rules and Duality Theorems
description: For a primal–dual pair in linear programming, construct the dual by transposing the constraint matrix, interchanging the objective coefficients and the right-hand sides of the constraints, and reversing the optimization direction: a minimization primal corresponds to a maximization dual. The dual of the dual returns to the primal. Weak duality states the ordering relation between the objective value of every dual-feasible solution and the optimal value, while strong duality states that the two problems have equal optimal values when the relevant optimal solutions exist. In multiple-choice questions, each statement about the dual construction must be checked separately and precisely.
applicability: A problem asks for the dual of a linear program or for a judgment about primal–dual conversion.
The question concerns the transpose of the constraint matrix, the destination of the right-hand side, objective coefficients, or the optimization direction.
Weak duality or strong duality is needed to compare feasible objective values or optimal values.

steps.step: Identify the primal matrix, coefficients, and optimization direction
steps.detail: Record the constraint matrix, the objective-function coefficient vector, the right-hand-side vector, the inequality directions, and whether the primal is a minimization or maximization problem.

steps.step: Construct the dual component by component
steps.detail: Transpose the constraint matrix; exchange the roles of the primal objective coefficients and constraint right-hand sides; and reverse the optimization direction, so a minimization primal has a maximization dual.

steps.step: Check the dual-of-dual relation
steps.detail: Verify that applying the construction a second time returns the original primal problem, including its matrix orientation, coefficients, directions, and optimization type.

steps.step: Apply weak and strong duality precisely
steps.detail: Use weak duality for the inequality between the objective value of a dual-feasible solution and the appropriate optimum, and use strong duality only for equality of the two optimal values under its conditions.

steps.step: Audit verbal statements one by one
steps.detail: Do not accept an imprecise claim such as ‘the objective function becomes a constraint.’ The primal objective coefficients become the right-hand sides of dual constraints; the primal constraint right-hand sides enter the dual objective; and the constraint matrix itself is transposed.

name: Translation-Invariant Total Orders and Parity Analysis of Rank Functions
description: A bijection with translation-order-preserving behavior is equivalent to a translation-invariant total order. Such an order is determined by a positive cone and can be represented as layers of a linear functional together with a tie-breaking rule inside every layer. Its rank function decomposes into a layer count plus an in-layer offset. This decomposition permits exact parity counting of ranks on a target rectangular region. One must range over the feasible parameter family consisting of coprime slopes and tie-breaking rules and optimize over that family. The count N varies with the coprime parameters (p,q) and the tie-breaking direction between N_min and N_max; the two extremes are attained by the two tie-breaking choices for an extreme slope of type (1,q). If the requested quantity is a product or combination of endpoint values, both endpoints must be found by traversing the parameter family rather than evaluating only one parameter choice.
applicability: A problem concerns an order-preserving bijection that is invariant under translations, or an equivalent translation-invariant total order.
The order is described by a coprime linear-functional slope (p,q) and an in-layer tie-breaking rule such as smaller x first versus smaller y first.
The task counts even or odd rank values on a rectangular target region, especially one with half-open interval boundaries.
The required result depends on extrema over all admissible order parameters.

steps.step: Replace the order-preserving bijection by a translation-invariant total order
steps.detail: Use the equivalence in the correct direction: the translation-order-preserving bijection induces a translation-invariant total order, and conversely the order determines the corresponding ranking behavior.

steps.step: Parameterize the order by layers and a tie-break
steps.detail: Choose a linear functional with coprime slope parameters (p,q), use its values as layer indices, and specify the in-layer rule, for example whether smaller x or smaller y is placed first.

steps.step: Decompose the rank function
steps.detail: Write each rank as the number of points in earlier layers plus the offset within the current layer. Keep these two terms separate when computing parity.

steps.step: Count parity by layer index and offset
steps.detail: For every point in the target rectangle, classify the parity of the layer contribution and the in-layer offset, then combine the two parities. Respect half-open boundary conventions exactly.

steps.step: Optimize over all feasible parameters
steps.detail: Compute the count for each admissible coprime slope and each tie-breaking direction. The values range from N_min to N_max, with endpoint values attained by the two tie-breaks for an extreme slope of type (1,q); do not infer the answer from a single parameter setting.

name: Digit DP for Divisibility Counting with Restricted Digit Sets
description: To count natural numbers whose number of digits is at most a specified bound, whose digits belong to a finite digit set, and whose value satisfies divisibility by a small modulus, use digit-by-digit dynamic programming. The state is the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or numerical value, and transitions are performed one digit at a time. Transition coefficients are determined by the residues modulo the modulus contributed by digits in the allowed set. The key distinction is between counting strings that allow leading zeroes and counting genuine natural numbers: the leading digit cannot be zero. The correction is: the number of valid natural numbers of length L equals the number of valid strings of length L minus the number of valid strings of length L−1. Finally, treat whether 0 itself is included according to the problem statement.
applicability: The three features ‘restricted digit set + divisibility by a small integer + bounded digit length’ occur together.
The modulus is small, often a one-digit integer, so remainder can be used directly as a DP-state dimension.
Several allowed digits can have the same residue modulo the modulus, allowing transitions to be compressed by residue frequency.

steps.step: Recognize the digit-DP structure
steps.detail: When the digit set is finite, the number must be divisible by a small modulus, and the number of digits has an upper bound, use a position-by-position DP rather than direct enumeration of strings.

steps.step: Define a remainder state
steps.detail: Track the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or processed numerical value, using the update rule appropriate to the divisibility condition.

steps.step: Compress transitions by digit residues
steps.detail: For every allowed digit, compute its residue modulo the modulus. If multiple digits have the same residue, count the number of occurrences of each residue first and use those counts as transition coefficients.

steps.step: Count strings with leading zeroes first
steps.detail: Run the DP for length L while allowing zero in every position to obtain the count of valid digit strings of length L.

steps.step: Correct to genuine natural numbers
steps.detail: Because the first digit of a natural number cannot be zero, use valid_natural_numbers(L) = valid_strings(L) − valid_strings(L−1). Sum the required lengths from 1 to the specified upper bound with correct endpoints.

steps.step: Handle zero and boundary cases
steps.detail: Check separately whether 0 is included by the problem statement. Avoid direct string enumeration without remainder classes, omitted leading-zero correction, and off-by-one errors in the length summation.

name: Classification of Integer-Valued Functions Under Divisibility Constraints
description: If an integer-valued function g satisfies the condition that, for every pair of distinct integers a,b, the difference g(a)−g(b) divides the corresponding difference of powers, then all solutions have power-function-family form: g is x raised to the d-th power, where d ranges over the divisors of the specified positive integer, or a mirror/translation variant of such a power function. When the exponent and power satisfy particular parity conditions, there is an additional signed family. The number of functions is twice the number of divisors when the exponent contains no factor 2. When it contains a power-of-2 factor, writing the exponent as its 2-adic part times its odd part gives twice the product of twice the 2-adic exponent and the number of divisors of the odd part. The condition that this number is 2 times an odd integer is equivalent to the divisor count being odd, hence to the positive integer being a perfect square. Combined with the parity constraint, this frequently reduces to odd perfect squares.
applicability: An integer-valued function is constrained by divisibility of differences g(a)−g(b) by differences of powers for all distinct integers a,b.
The task requires classification of all functions, counting the families, or locating the N-th positive integer with a stated count property.
The exponent has parity or 2-adic structure relevant to the number of solution families.

steps.step: Identify the standard function families
steps.detail: Start from the power functions g(x)=x^d for every divisor d of the specified positive integer, together with their mirror/translation variants.

steps.step: Separate the parity branch
steps.detail: Analyze the specified parity relation between exponent and power. Include the additional signed solution family when that parity condition holds; do not omit it.

steps.step: Establish the exact counting formula
steps.detail: If the exponent has no factor 2, the total is 2 times the divisor count. If it has a 2-adic factor and an odd part, use 2 times twice the 2-adic exponent times the divisor count of the odd part.

steps.step: Convert the requested count property into a divisor property
steps.detail: Use count = 2 × odd if and only if the divisor count is odd, which holds if and only if the integer is a perfect square. Combine this with any parity restriction.

steps.step: Invert an ordinal only after deriving the sequence
steps.detail: For the resulting odd-perfect-square sequence, the N-th term is (2N−1)^2. Check N=1,2,3, obtaining 1,9,25, before substituting the requested ordinal; do not use N^2 directly.

name: Prime Divisibility in Recurrences and Coprime Linear-Combination Norms
description: Two recurring lines of argument are useful. (a) For coprime integers k,l, the coefficient-norm function defined by min |a|+|b| subject to ka+lb=x measures the shortest representation of an integer with respect to the generating pair. The number of ‘nice’ integers satisfying a local-maximum condition depends only on the smaller parameter and on the parity case: both parameters odd versus one parameter even. The corresponding counting formulas differ by a multiplicative factor arising from symmetry. (b) To prove that every prime divides some term of a linear recurrence, first derive its closed form as a homogeneous solution plus a particular solution, reducing it to a power sum plus a constant. Then use Fermat's little theorem and modular periodicity to find, for every prime, an exponent index at which that prime divides the designated term. In the norm-equation ending, reduce to (αy−βd)^2+γt^2=δd^2; solution parity is determined by a divisibility condition of type 14|d, and typical counts simplify as F=l−1 and G=2(l−1), giving a target expression of type p^2+q^2=5(l−1)^2 for l.
applicability: Coprime coefficients k,l define representations ka+lb=x and the objective is min |a|+|b| or a local-extremum count.
A recurrence must be shown to have a term divisible by every prime.
A statement about integers coprime to all terms needs reduction to prime factors and separate modular arguments.
The final calculation reduces to a quadratic or imaginary-quadratic norm equation with parity and divisibility conditions.

steps.step: Treat the coefficient norm as the primary object
steps.detail: For ka+lb=x with gcd(k,l)=1, study min |a|+|b| as a function of x rather than attempting only isolated Diophantine solutions.

steps.step: Separate parity cases before counting
steps.detail: Derive the count for the cases ‘both k and l odd’ and ‘one even’ separately. The ratio between the formulas follows from symmetry; combining the cases prematurely gives an incorrect proportion.

steps.step: Derive the recurrence closed form exactly
steps.detail: Solve the recurrence as homogeneous solution plus particular solution, retaining the constant term and all coefficients, and rewrite it as a power sum plus a constant.

steps.step: Prove prime divisibility uniformly
steps.detail: For each prime, use Fermat's little theorem and modular periodicity to select an exponent index for which the designated recurrence term is divisible by that prime. Do not extrapolate from checks of a few small primes, and do not confuse ‘every prime divides some term’ with ‘one prime divides every term.’

steps.step: Complete the norm-equation count
steps.detail: Reduce the coefficient-norm relation to (αy−βd)^2+γt^2=δd^2. Use a condition of type 14|d to decide solution parity, then apply F=l−1 and G=2(l−1) when those counts arise, yielding the target form p^2+q^2=5(l−1)^2.

name: Floor Inequalities via Complete Residue Systems
description: For inequalities required to hold in every residue class, change the traversal index so that it runs from 1 to p−1 and use the complete-residue-system property modulo a prime p: after setting j=k+1, the residues of n·j modulo p still run through all nonzero residue classes. Rewrite the inequality as a condition that, for every j, the residue is at least a linear threshold. Via residue = original quantity − modulus × floor, this is equivalent to a uniform upper bound on a floor quotient. All admissible n form the decreasing sequence of floor values ⌊p/j⌋ for consecutive integers j. Therefore the k-th largest admissible value is ⌊p/k⌋. This conclusion requires explicit verification for k=1,2 and correct treatment of repeated values in the floor sequence.
applicability: An inequality is required for every residue class modulo a prime p.
Replacing k by j=k+1 converts the relevant terms into a complete nonzero residue system.
The problem asks for an upper bound on floor quotients or for the k-th largest admissible integer.

steps.step: Reindex the nonzero residues
steps.detail: Set j=k+1 so the index traverses 1 through p−1. When n<p, multiplication by n permutes the nonzero residues modulo the prime p; this prerequisite must be checked.

steps.step: Rewrite through quotient and remainder
steps.detail: Let r=nj mod p. Use r = nj − p⌊nj/p⌋ to convert the lower bound on r into the required uniform upper bound for a floor expression. Preserve the inequality direction.

steps.step: Identify the complete admissible sequence
steps.detail: The admissible n are exactly the decreasing values of the form ⌊p/j⌋ as j=1,2,3,… increases.

steps.step: Locate the requested rank
steps.detail: The k-th largest value is ⌊p/k⌋. Check k=1 and k=2 by writing the two largest admissible values before applying the general formula; ⌊p/(k+1)⌋ is the common one-position error.

steps.step: Account for repeated floors
steps.detail: The sequence ⌊p/j⌋ can contain repeated values, so count ranks using the ordered sequence and its multiplicities rather than treating all quotient values as distinct.

name: Digit Structure in Long Division with Zero-Free Dividends
description: For division with remainder in which the dividend has a fixed number of decimal digits and no zero digit, analyze the decimal structure of the quotient. If the quotient has L digits and t nonzero digits, and the divisor has d digits, view multiplication as the position-shifted superposition of one copy of the divisor for every nonzero quotient digit. These copies must cover every digit position of the dividend without producing a zero digit, yielding a coverage inequality relating t·d and L. Maximizing the number A=L−t of zero digits in the quotient becomes a discrete optimization that balances L and t under the digit budget. If L is too large, each copy covers too little; if L is too small, digits are wasted. At the optimum, nonzero quotient digits are approximately equally spaced. One must still verify whether carries fill the gaps and how the remainder corrects the last digit. The closing bound is t·d≥L, followed by a construction with nonuniform gaps and carry filling, and a proof that if A+1 gaps are too large they cannot be filled (the 939-type ending).
applicability: A fixed-length dividend with no zero digit is divided with remainder, and the task asks about zero versus nonzero digits of the quotient.
The divisor digit length d, quotient length L, and number t of nonzero quotient digits can be related by shifted multiplication copies.
A sharp upper bound and a construction attaining it are both required.

steps.step: Use the shifted-copy coverage view
steps.detail: Expand quotient times divisor as one d-digit divisor copy for each nonzero quotient digit, shifted according to that digit's position.

steps.step: Derive the coverage inequality
steps.detail: Because the copies must cover the full dividend without creating zero positions, obtain t·d≥L. Treat this as an inequality, not an equality.

steps.step: Optimize the zero count discretely
steps.detail: Set A=L−t and optimize over feasible integer values of L and t. Balance the loss from overly large L against wasted digit budget from overly small L.

steps.step: Construct near-equally spaced nonzero digits
steps.detail: Use approximately equal spacing, allowing nonuniform gaps where necessary, and verify that carries can fill the intervening positions and that the remainder corrects the final digit.

steps.step: Prove optimality in the opposite direction
steps.detail: After the construction reaches the candidate bound, prove that A+1 gaps would be too large to fill, using the 939-type terminal argument. Do not give a construction without an upper-bound proof.

name: Line Covers of Planar Point Sets and an Erdős–de Bruijn-Type Bound
description: Consider a planar point set S which cannot be covered altogether by a specified number of lines, has no circle through all its points, but becomes coverable by the same number of lines after deletion of any one point. To maximize |S|, take a family of lines in general position—no two parallel and no three concurrent—and let S be the set of all pairwise intersections. After one intersection is deleted, every remaining intersection lies on the lines other than the two that determined the deleted point, so the deletion-cover condition holds automatically. The absence of a circle through all points is an additional condition that must be verified separately. An Erdős–de Bruijn-type theorem gives a quadratic-in-the-number-of-lines upper bound for such covering conditions, and the number of pairwise intersections in the construction attains that bound.
applicability: A point set is globally not coverable by a prescribed number of lines, while deletion of any one point makes it coverable by that same number.
The problem includes an additional nonconcyclicity condition.
A maximum cardinality is sought under line-cover incidence constraints.

steps.step: Recognize the intersection-set construction
steps.detail: The symmetric condition ‘not coverable as a whole, but coverable after deletion of any point’ suggests taking all pairwise intersections of a line family.

steps.step: Impose general position
steps.detail: Require no parallel lines and no three lines through one point. Otherwise both the intersection count and the deletion-cover structure change.

steps.step: Verify the deletion-cover condition
steps.detail: When an intersection determined by two lines is removed, retain all the other lines; every other pairwise intersection lies on at least one retained line.

steps.step: Check the independent circle condition
steps.detail: Explicitly rule out a circle passing through all chosen intersections; it is not implied by the covering argument.

steps.step: Match construction with the upper bound
steps.detail: Use point–line incidence counting or an Erdős–de Bruijn-type theorem to obtain the quadratic upper bound in the number of lines. When it equals the pairwise-intersection count, the construction is extremal.

name: Angle Subdivision and Segment Ratios in a Right Triangle
description: In a right triangle, choose two points on one leg so that the endpoint of the hypotenuse subtends prescribed split angles at those points, and determine the ratio of the two intercepted segments. Decompose the diagram according to the positions of the two subtended angles into two small triangles. In each triangle, use the sine rule to express the target segment as the adjacent leg or hypotenuse divided by the sine of its corresponding angle. Then use right-triangle relations—complementary acute angles and the interchange of sine and cosine—to express both segments in terms of one reference length. Finally simplify the sine ratio with a double-angle identity. The resulting ratio is independent of the size of the original triangle and is a constant.
applicability: A right triangle contains two points on a leg, with given angle subdivision at the hypotenuse endpoint.
The task asks for a ratio of segments cut off by rays rather than an absolute length.
The prescribed angles permit sine-rule evaluation and double-angle simplification.

steps.step: Draw and order the subtended rays correctly
steps.detail: The order of the two points determines the geometric angle configuration. Mark the two rays from the hypotenuse endpoint before assigning angles.

steps.step: Apply the sine rule in each small triangle
steps.detail: For each target segment, pair every side with its opposite angle exactly; express it through the relevant adjacent leg or hypotenuse and a sine ratio.

steps.step: Move to a common reference length
steps.detail: Use complementary acute angles in the right triangle to interchange sine and cosine as needed, so both segment expressions use the same base length.

steps.step: Simplify the ratio trigonometrically
steps.detail: Cancel the common length and use the required double-angle formula, retaining all coefficients.

steps.step: Check orientation and numerator order
steps.detail: Verify the requested numerator and denominator against the statement. A reversed point order, mismatched opposite angle, or omitted double-angle coefficient invalidates the result.

name: Distribution of Vertex Area-Bisectors in a Convex Polygon
description: In a convex polygon, draw from every vertex the segment that bisects the polygonal area and meets the opposite boundary. The distribution of the resulting endpoints is controlled by a continuity-and-partition argument: as the area-bisector continuously sweeps the polygon, the boundary edges receiving endpoints from the vertices form at most a constant number of consecutive blocks in boundary order. Consequently all endpoints lie on at most three edges, independently of the number n of polygon sides. The minimum is therefore the constant 3: for n=3 this is the median case, and for n≥4 a nearly degenerate construction attains exactly three receiving edges. The area bisector need not pass through the midpoint of the opposite side.
applicability: A convex n-gon has one area-bisecting segment from each vertex to the opposite boundary.
The problem asks for the smallest possible number of boundary edges containing all intersection endpoints.
Continuity and boundary-order arguments can show that the quantity is independent of n.

steps.step: Distinguish an area bisector from a median
steps.detail: The segment halves polygonal area but is not required to pass through the midpoint of its opposite boundary side.

steps.step: Use continuous sweeping along the boundary
steps.detail: Track the endpoint of the vertex area-bisector as the relevant vertex position varies. Use continuity to organize receiving edges into consecutive boundary segments.

steps.step: Count receiving-edge blocks in boundary order
steps.detail: The continuity partition bounds all endpoints by three edges. Include cases in which an endpoint coincides with a polygon vertex so no edge is over- or under-counted.

steps.step: Prove the lower bound constructively
steps.detail: For n=3 use the median configuration. For every n≥4 give a nearly degenerate convex construction in which endpoints occur on exactly three edges.

steps.step: State the n-independent optimum
steps.detail: The minimum is 3 for all n; it is a constant, not a function of n.

name: Compatibility of Congruent Triangle Dissections and Tangential Polygons
description: When a convex polygon is dissected by nonintersecting diagonals into congruent triangles, the dissection structure—the number of triangles and the number of triangle angles meeting at every vertex—is determined by the number of sides. Congruence forces every polygonal interior angle to be an integer-multiple allocation of one common set of triangle angles. If the polygon must also be tangential to a circle, hence possess an incircle, it must satisfy the equality of sums of opposite sides or concurrence of angle bisectors. The two requirements are compatible only in the smallest side-number case: the symmetry forced by the congruent dissection gives a kite, and imposing the tangency condition forces all four sides equal, producing a special quadrilateral that always has an incircle. For larger numbers of sides, exclude possibilities case by case using total angle measure or broken symmetry.
applicability: A convex polygon is triangulated by pairwise nonintersecting diagonals into congruent triangles.
The polygon is additionally required to be tangential, meaning that it has an incircle rather than merely a circumcircle.
The goal is to determine all feasible numbers of sides.

steps.step: Write the dissection angle-allocation equations
steps.detail: Use the number of congruent triangles and the number of triangle angles incident at each polygon vertex to express each interior angle as an integer-multiple allocation.

steps.step: Apply the correct tangency criterion
steps.detail: For a tangential polygon use equality of opposite-side sums or concurrence of angle bisectors. Do not confuse this with cyclicity, which concerns a circumcircle.

steps.step: Construct the smallest feasible case
steps.detail: In the smallest side-number case, the congruent dissection enforces kite symmetry; after imposing tangency, all four sides are forced equal, giving the special quadrilateral with an incircle.

steps.step: Exclude larger side counts
steps.detail: For each larger number of sides, use the total angle sum or the failure of the required symmetry to rule out compatibility.

steps.step: Check every vertex separately
steps.detail: Congruent triangles can contribute different numbers of angles at different polygon vertices, so verify each interior-angle sum rather than assuming uniform incidence.

name: Angle-Multiple Relations and Solution Counts in a Collinear Configuration
description: Choose a moving point on the line containing a segment so that two subtended angles satisfy a multiple relation, with one angle exactly half the other. Geometrically this is a ray-trisection picture. Convert every ratio relation by the sine rule or similarity into an equation for the position of the moving point, measured as a distance from the intersection. Once the inclination of the fixed line is fixed, every relation has at most one solution on each ray, that is, on each of the two directions from the point. There are two possible angle relations and two ray directions, giving an upper bound of 4. All four solutions occur when the endpoint-distance ratio lies in a compatibility interval of type (1/2,2) and the line inclination is suitable; outside that interval the number can drop abruptly.
applicability: A moving point lies on the line of a segment, and two subtended angles have a 2-to-1 relation.
The task asks for the number or maximum number of geometric solutions.
Endpoint distances from an intersection and the inclination of a fixed line determine compatibility.

steps.step: Separate the two angle relations
steps.detail: ‘The larger angle is twice the smaller’ and its reversed placement are different cases and must both be considered.

steps.step: Split the line into two rays
steps.detail: A moving point can occur in either direction from the intersection. For each fixed relation, prove there is at most one solution per ray.

steps.step: Convert to a position equation
steps.detail: Use the sine rule or similar triangles to rewrite the angle-ratio condition as an equation in the distance from the intersection.

steps.step: Check simultaneous compatibility
steps.detail: Determine when solutions from all relations and both directions coexist. The endpoint-distance ratio must lie in an interval of type (1/2,2), and the inclination must be appropriate.

steps.step: Establish and attain the maximum
steps.detail: Two relations times two directions gives at most 4 solutions. Give a compatible configuration attaining 4 rather than merely counting the upper bound.

name: Face Visibility of Convex Polyhedra via Normal-Vector Separation
description: From an exterior observation point, a face of a convex polyhedron is visible exactly when its outward normal has positive dot product with the viewing direction. Requiring that every face have an observation point from which all other faces are visible while that face alone is hidden is equivalent to requiring that each face normal be separable from all other normals by a hyperplane through the origin. In three dimensions this property is possible only for a simplex normal configuration, dual to a tetrahedron. Hence the minimum possible number of faces is 4. For a tetrahedron, verify the construction face by face by choosing, for every face, an observation point close to that face and outside the other three faces. The point must lie strictly in the exterior half-space of the hidden face.
applicability: A convex polyhedron is viewed from exterior points and a visibility condition isolates one hidden face at a time.
The problem asks for a minimum number of faces under visibility constraints.
Face visibility can be converted to dot products of outward normals and linear separation.

steps.step: Translate visibility into normal-vector inequalities
steps.detail: A face is visible when its outward normal has positive dot product with the viewing direction. Encode the condition for every face separately.

steps.step: Formulate individual hiding as origin-hyperplane separation
steps.detail: For each normal, require a hyperplane through the origin that separates it from all the remaining normals; this is equivalent to hiding precisely the corresponding face while seeing the others.

steps.step: Apply the simplex configuration bound
steps.detail: Use convex-cone or separation results, such as Carathéodory-type reasoning, to show that a three-dimensional configuration with this property is a simplex normal configuration.

steps.step: Construct and verify the tetrahedron
steps.detail: The resulting minimum is 4. For each tetrahedral face choose a point close to it on its exterior side, and check that this face alone is hidden while the other three are visible.

steps.step: Check strictness and quantifiers
steps.detail: Do not merely find a point seeing most faces: every face must be individually hideable. The observation point must be strictly outside the half-space of the face being hidden.

name: Common Points of Three Circles and Parametric Tangent Circles
description: For a parameterized family of circles, three circles have exactly two common points precisely when each pair meets in the same pair of points, equivalently when the circles are coaxal. Test this through coincident common chords or concurrent radical axes. If one circle passes through a fixed point and is tangent to a fixed circle at a prescribed tangency point, its center lies on the normal through that tangency point, and its radius is uniquely determined by the fixed point. Thus the center and radius of the family are explicit functions of the parameter. Write the coaxality condition algebraically and solve for every parameter value. In the unit-circumcircle coordinate setup, scan the coaxality discriminant over values such as k∈[0.1,3] to locate candidates k=1/2 and k=1, then supply the geometric proof through midpoint and excenter configurations. The answer commonly consists of two fractional values, both of which must be reported.
applicability: A family of circles is constrained by a fixed point and tangency to a fixed circle at a specified point.
The task asks for all parameter values for which three circles have exactly two common points.
Radical-axis or common-chord criteria can be converted into an algebraic condition.

steps.step: Distinguish two common points from one common point
steps.detail: Exactly two common points means pairwise intersections in one common pair, not merely that all three circles share one point. Treat a tangent double intersection according to the problem's counting convention.

steps.step: Parameterize center and radius
steps.detail: Place the center on the normal line through the fixed tangency point; use the condition of passing through the fixed point to determine the radius explicitly.

steps.step: Write a coaxality criterion
steps.detail: Use coincident common chords, concurrent radical axes, or an algebraic coaxality determinant for the three circle equations.

steps.step: Find and prove every parameter value
steps.detail: In a unit-circumcircle coordinate computation, use a scan of the discriminant, for example k∈[0.1,3], only to identify candidates such as k=1/2 and k=1; then prove them geometrically via midpoint or excenter configurations.

steps.step: Check degeneracies
steps.detail: Verify tangency directions, the fixed normal, special internal-division ratios, symmetric degeneracies, and whether all candidate fractional values satisfy the stated ‘exactly two’ condition.

name: Tangents, Arc Midpoints, and Angle Closure on the Circumcircle of a Right Triangle
description: The circumcircle of a right triangle has the hypotenuse as a diameter by Thales' theorem. In the configuration chain ‘a tangent at a vertex meets the extension of the opposite side; take the midpoint of the minor arc; join it and meet the circle again; a tangent at the new intersection meets the other leg; determine an angle,’ repeatedly use three tools: an arc midpoint is equidistant from arc endpoints and gives the corresponding angle-bisector relation; the tangent–chord angle theorem; and the fact that an angle subtended by a diameter is a right angle. The angle chain often closes to a right angle independently of the triangle's shape. A coordinate method placing the circumcenter at the origin and the hypotenuse on an axis converts the chain into line–circle intersections, with angles read from slopes or vector dot products.

For a moving point outside the circles, draw its three polar lines; they form a triangle, and study the relation between the circumcircle of that triangle and the moving point. The orthocenter M lies on all three circles because each radius was defined as the distance to M. name: Convex Quadrilateral Area via Diagonals and Perimeter-Constrained Optimization

name: Latin Squares with Inter-Row Difference Constraints
description: Fill a table row by row with permutations of n symbols, requiring each row to be a permutation and each column to have distinct entries; this is a Latin square. Column distinctness immediately bounds the number of rows by n. A condition that any two rows have a difference at least a prescribed threshold in at least one column excludes pairs of adjacent permutations, namely pairs whose entrywise differences are all too small to meet the threshold. When the row count reaches its maximum, the table is an n×n Latin square, and the required enumeration is the number of Latin squares satisfying the difference condition. Fixing the first row removes the full-row permutation symmetry before counting. The condition means ‘at least one column meets the threshold,’ not ‘every column meets it.’

name: Pairwise Product-Sum Identity and an Optimal Lower Bound
description: For a real tuple, rewrite the sum of pairwise products through the identity Σ_{p<q} c_p c_q=[(Σc)^2−Σc^2]/2. name: Special-Value Substitution and Polynomialization of Functional Equations
description: For a two-variable functional equation, first substitute special values that eliminate one variable, such as zero or a unit, to obtain one-variable constraints. This either rules out constant candidates or fixes critical initial values. Then substitute paired values such as opposites and subtract the resulting equations to eliminate terms at antipodal points, yielding a recurrence. Use it to prove that every solution is a polynomial with bounded degree. Finally write a general polynomial, compare coefficients to get a finite candidate list, and substitute every candidate back into the original equation. Both necessity—no other solutions—and sufficiency—each candidate works—must be established.
applicability: A functional equation has two variables and special substitutions can remove one of them.
Opposite or paired arguments permit subtraction that eliminates symmetric terms.
The objective is to classify all solutions, often by proving they are polynomials of controlled degree.

name: Edge-Flip Propagation on Rational Graphs and Continued-Fraction Reduction
description: Let a function on the rational numbers take values in a binary field and require unequal values at the two ends of each of three edge types: negation, complement, and reciprocal. The value at one point determines the entire function uniquely by connectivity of the graph; edge flips are exactly a graph two-coloring. To evaluate the function at an arbitrary rational, reduce it by a continued-fraction/Euclidean procedure: repeatedly subtract the integer part, which does not change the function value, and take the reciprocal, which flips the value, until reaching a constant. The parity of the number of reciprocal operations determines whether the value agrees with the initial value or is flipped. Finally sum values in the binary field, using parity arithmetic rather than decimal carrying.
applicability: A rational-valued graph has negation, complement, and reciprocal edges, and a binary-valued function flips across every such edge.
The task asks for values at rationals or their binary-field sum.
Continued fractions or Euclidean reduction can reduce each rational to a base point.

name: Logarithmic Differentiation and Partial Fractions for Excluding Real Roots
description: For a real-coefficient polynomial F, use logarithmic differentiation to expand F′/F as the partial-fraction sum of reciprocals of the roots. Differentiating again gives (F′/F)′=(F″F−F′²)/F² and hence F″F−F′²=−F²·Σ1/(z−α)^2. For real z away from the roots this is strictly negative, as the expression is the negative of a sum of squares times F². At a simple root, F=0 but F′≠0, so the sign can also be determined directly. Thus equations containing products of F and its first and second derivatives can be shown to have no real solutions without knowing the individual roots. Root points and nonroot intervals must be handled separately.

name: Polynomial Invariants Under Parameter Transformations
description: When a bivariate polynomial f is required to take equal values on two classes of parameter points, first translate the correspondence between points into a coordinate transformation. If that transformation preserves two basic symmetric invariants—a sum-type invariant and an invariant constructed from a product and a squared difference—then two parameter points lie in the same orbit if and only if both invariants agree. The full solution set is exactly the ring of polynomials expressible in these two invariants. Prove both directions: every solution satisfying the original condition must be a polynomial in the invariant generators, and every polynomial in those generators satisfies the condition.

name: Power Reduction and Minimal Polynomials in a Cubic Radical Extension
description: For a number x that is the sum of two cubic radicals, choose a basis of the extension and reduce every cube of an individual radical to a constant. Repeated power reduction expresses every power of x as a linear combination of basis elements, yielding an integer-coefficient polynomial equation for x and hence its minimal polynomial. To find a polynomial for a target quantity such as x divided by one radical, first express that quantity in basis coordinates. Then take an undetermined polynomial of the lowest feasible degree, expand its value in the same basis, and compare coordinates. Linear independence of the basis gives a linear system for the coefficients; solve it and substitute back to verify. One must compute the multiplication table correctly, retain cross terms in powers of x, continually reduce higher powers into the basis, and prove that the degree cannot be lowered further.

name: Solution Orbits and Counting for Symmetric Polynomial Systems
description: For a cyclically symmetric multivariable polynomial system, first exploit the fact that cyclic permutations and simultaneous sign reversal preserve the solution set. Find the basic fully symmetric solutions with all variables equal, then use Bézout's theorem only as an upper bound. Eliminate variables through a resultant or Gröbner basis to obtain a high-degree univariate equation. Count its real roots and organize them into symmetry orbits: every nonsymmetric solution comes with its three cyclic permutations and their simultaneous sign reversals, forming an orbit of size 6. In the stated eighth-degree reduction, the count is 2 fully symmetric solutions plus one nonsymmetric orbit of size 3×2=6, for 8 real solutions. Elimination may introduce components not belonging to the original system, so every counted root must be checked back in the system.

name: Closure Generated by Vector Addition and Coordinatewise Maximum
description: For integer vectors with both addition and coordinatewise maximum allowed, the set generated by initial vectors has a lattice-plus-semilattice structure.
